source_refs.note: iv. Oxidation of alcohols: a main subheading of 22.4 Reactions of Alcohols, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 92-92.

blocks.text: Primary alcohols can be oxidised to form aldehydes and the secondary alcohols can be oxidised to form only ketones using oxidizing agents. Tertiary alcohols do not undergo oxidation. The oxidising agents for alcohols include acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ and acidified KMnO₄. Acidified potassium chromate(VI), K₂Cr₂O₇, is an orange oxidising agent. When alcohols are oxidised the orange dichromate ions (Cr₂O₇²⁻) are reduced to green Cr³⁺ ions.

blocks.title: Keep in Mind
blocks.text: For potassium dichromate(VI) to act as an oxidising agent, it must first be reduced. This reduction requires hydrogen (H⁺) ions which are provided by the acidic medium.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: K₂Cr₂O₇ is potassium dichromate(VI), not potassium chromate(VI) (which is K₂CrO₄), as the book itself names it in the same paragraph and in the Keep in Mind box.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The label under ethanol is printed 'ethonal'; it is ethanol.

Therefore, only the oxidation of primary and secondary alcohols will change the colour of acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ solution as the orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ ions are reduced to green Cr³⁺ ions, which is used to check the presence of primary or secondary alcohol.

Only propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol, which are primary and secondary alcohols respectively, can get oxidised, turning the orange solution green; no colour change is observed with 2-methyl-propan-2-ol, which is a tertiary alcohol.

blocks.alt: Three test tubes of acidified potassium dichromate: propan-1-ol (primary alcohol) dark green, propan-2-ol (secondary alcohol) dark green, and 2-methyl-propan-2-ol (tertiary alcohol) orange.
blocks.caption: Acidified potassium dichromate with primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 94).

blocks.title: Interesting Information
blocks.text: Driving after consuming alcohol is very dangerous. A breathalyser is a device that is used by the traffic officers to check if a driver is drunk or not. This device uses the oxidation of ethanol, which requires electrons. The amount of current used is proportional to the amount of alcohol consumed.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Oxidation releases electrons; it does not require them. In the breathalyser the ethanol in the breath is oxidised, and the electrons it gives up make the current that is measured; the current is proportional to the amount of alcohol.
